code.title: Cache-friendly vs cache-hostile traversal: same work, same answer

followUps:
The three Cs are compulsory, capacity and conflict misses. A compulsory miss is the first touch of a line, so it cannot be avoided except by prefetching. A capacity miss happens because the working set is bigger than the cache, so lines are evicted and fetched again. A conflict miss happens when many lines map to the same set and push each other out although the cache has free space elsewhere.

Example: summing a 1 MB array in a 32 KB L1 gives capacity misses on every repeat pass. Fix with blocking (tiling) so each tile fits in cache.

The prefetcher watches the stream of addresses and guesses the next lines from the pattern, then loads them before the program asks. It tracks sequential access (next-line), constant strides (it learns that every 256 bytes is touched) and per-instruction patterns.

Example: a loop reading a[0], a[16], a[32] (stride 64 bytes) is detected after two or three accesses and later lines arrive early. Random or pointer-chasing access has no pattern, so nothing is prefetched and each miss costs the full DRAM latency. Prefetchers also do not cross 4 KB page boundaries, so a stream restarts there.

A power-of-two stride makes many addresses map to the same cache set, so they fight for a few ways while other sets sit empty. The set index comes from the middle address bits, and a stride like 4096 leaves those bits unchanged.

Example: a 32 KB, 8-way L1 with 64-byte lines has 64 sets. Reading a column of a 1024-float matrix (4096-byte rows) touches addresses 4096 apart, all in one set. After 8 rows the lines evict each other, so column walks keep missing. Fix: pad each row (e.g. 1024+16 floats) so the stride is not a power of two.

code.title: Struct padding: sizeof, offsets and reordering

followUps:
An empty class has size 1, because every object must have a unique address and a size of 0 would let two distinct objects share one address. The compiler therefore adds one byte.

Example: struct E{}; E a, b; gives sizeof(E)==1 and &a != &b. An array E arr[3] is 3 bytes. When an empty class is used as a base class, the empty base optimisation lets it take zero space, which is why std::vector implementations can store an empty allocator for free. As a member, an empty object still costs at least a byte plus padding unless you mark it [[no_unique_address]].

[[no_unique_address]] (C++20) allows a data member to share its address with other members, so an empty member can take no space. It is the member-level version of the empty base optimisation.

struct Empty {};
struct A { int x; Empty e; };                         // size 8
struct B { int x; [[no_unique_address]] Empty e; };   // size 4

The 4 bytes saved in A come from the byte for e plus the padding that realigns to 4. It matters for policy classes and stateless allocators or comparators stored inside containers. Note MSVC ignores the attribute and needs [[msvc::no_unique_address]].

Because padding bytes (and sometimes the value bits of types like floats) are not guaranteed to hold anything meaningful, two equal-looking structs can compare unequal with memcmp.

Example: struct S{char c; int i;}; has 3 padding bytes after c. Two objects with c='a', i=5 may hold different garbage in those bytes, so memcmp(&a,&b,sizeof(S)) may say they differ. Also 0.0 and -0.0 are equal but have different bits, and NaN is not equal to itself though bits match. Compare member by member, or use operator== (= default in C++20).

code.title: False sharing: packed vs cache-line-padded counters

followUps:
True sharing is when threads really use the same variable, so they must communicate; false sharing is when they use different variables that only happen to live in the same cache line. The slowdown looks the same, but the cure is different.

Example: two threads incrementing one shared counter is true sharing, and padding cannot help; you need an atomic, a lock or per-thread counters merged at the end. Two threads each incrementing their own counter, 8 bytes apart, is false sharing, and alignas(64) fixes it. Both cause cache-line ping-pong, but only false sharing is a pure layout bug.

Because the real size to avoid sharing is not always 64 bytes. Some CPUs fetch pairs of adjacent lines (a 128-byte unit), so two variables 64 bytes apart can still interfere. Recent Apple cores use 128-byte lines, and some Intel parts have an adjacent-line prefetcher.

Example: two counters at offsets 0 and 64 on a CPU with a 128-byte coherence granule still share a unit. Using std::hardware_destructive_interference_size gives the compiler's best guess, but it is fixed at compile time, so a binary built for one CPU may run on another. When unsure, pad to 128 and measure.

code.title: Branchy vs branchless sum on sorted and unsorted data

followUps:
Branchless code is slower when the branch is well predicted, because the branchless version always does the work of both sides while a predicted branch skips one side for free.

Example: if (x >= 128) sum += expensive(x) where only 1% of values qualify. The branchy version runs expensive 1% of the time at almost no misprediction cost. The branchless version computes expensive every time, maybe 50 times more work. Branchless wins when the branch is unpredictable (about 50/50) and the extra work is cheap, such as a select or a multiply. Measure with real data.

They are hints about which path is more likely. They mainly change code layout (the likely path falls straight through, the unlikely one is moved away), and can influence inlining and register allocation. They do not make the CPU predict differently, because modern hardware predictors learn from actual history and ignore compiler hints.

Example: marking an error path [[unlikely]] keeps the hot loop compact in the instruction cache. If your hint is wrong, you lose a little speed, but results never change. They are no substitute for PGO, which uses measured frequencies.

An indirect branch (a virtual call or function pointer) is predicted by an indirect target predictor that looks up the likely target from the branch address plus recent branch history. If one call site almost always reaches the same type, the guess is nearly perfect.

Example: a loop calling shape->area() over a vector of mixed Circle and Square in random order gives the predictor a changing target and many misses (~15-20 cycles each). Sorting the objects by type, or storing separate vectors per type, makes the target repeat and prediction succeeds. Compilers can also use PGO to add a guarded direct call for the common type.

code.title: inline: linkage, constexpr and noinline

followUps:
Because std::sort is a template, the comparison is known at compile time and gets inlined, while qsort calls a comparison function through a pointer for every comparison.

Example: sorting 1,000,000 ints takes about 20 million comparisons. With qsort, each is a real indirect call (pushing arguments, jumping, returning, taking void* and casting). With std::sort(v.begin(), v.end()) the comparison becomes a single machine compare in the loop, and the optimiser can also keep values in registers. In practice std::sort is often 2 to 3 times faster.

Link-time optimisation (LTO) lets the compiler see all translation units at link time, so it can inline a function defined in another .cpp file, which is impossible when each file is compiled alone.

Example: int get() { return x; } in a.cpp and a hot loop in b.cpp that calls it. Without LTO the loop pays a real call each iteration; with LTO the body is inlined and the loop may even be vectorised. The costs are longer link times and more memory. ThinLTO in Clang gives most of the gain with parallel, incremental builds.

Yes, when the compiler knows the exact dynamic type at the call, it can skip the vtable lookup and inline the body. This is called devirtualisation.

Dog d;
Animal& a = d;
a.speak();     // type known: direct call, can inline
std::unique_ptr<Animal> p = make();
p->speak();    // unknown: indirect call

It also works for final classes or methods (no overrides possible) and with PGO or LTO whole-program knowledge. If the type is only known at run time, the call stays indirect.

code.title: As-if rule: loop folding, dead store and constant folding

followUps:
-O3 adds more aggressive loop work: stronger unrolling, vectorisation of more loops, loop interchange, function cloning and more inlining. It is not always faster because the bigger code can overflow the instruction cache, and extra unrolling or vector prologue and epilogue code hurts short loops.

Example: a loop that runs 3 iterations gets vectorised with 8-wide SIMD, which adds a remainder loop and setup, so it becomes slower than -O2. Always benchmark both on real data.

-ffast-math lets the compiler ignore strict IEEE rules, so it can reorder floating-point operations and assume no NaN or infinity. That breaks exact results and error checks.

Example: floating-point addition is not associative: (1e16 + 1) - 1e16 is 0 in strict maths, but a reordered sum may give 1. It can also remove isnan(x) checks, turn x/y into x*(1/y), and change the order of a summation, so results differ between builds. Use it only where exact semantics do not matter, or enable specific flags such as -fno-math-errno.

PGO (profile-guided optimisation) uses real run data to decide inlining, branch layout and hot/cold code placement; BOLT is a post-link tool that reorders functions and basic blocks of the final binary using a profile.

Example: PGO learns that branch A is taken 99% of the time and places it on the fall-through path, and inlines hot call sites only. BOLT then lays out hot functions together to cut instruction-cache and iTLB misses. Typical gains on large server binaries are 5 to 20 percent. The cost is a more complex build, and the profile must match production traffic.

code.title: Implementation-defined, defined wrap and avoiding UB

followUps:
Because the compiler is allowed to assume UB never happens, it may transform or delete code before the faulty line that would only be valid if the faulty line were reached.

int f(int* p) {
  int x = *p;      // UB if p is null
  if (p == nullptr) return -1;
  return x;
}

Since *p already ran, the compiler concludes p is non-null and deletes the null check, so a null input does not return -1.

Because unsigned types were defined to wrap around modulo 2^N so hash and bit tricks work, while signed overflow was left undefined so compilers can optimise freely and support machines with different representations.

Example: with signed int i, the compiler can assume i + 1 > i is always true and drop the check, and can turn i*2/2 into i. For unsigned u = 4294967295u, u + 1 is 0 by definition, so these shortcuts are not allowed. The cost is slightly fewer loop optimisations for unsigned indexes.

code.title: Fixing the three UB examples

followUps:
ASan catches 2 of 3 clearly: the push_back reallocation (heap-use-after-free) and, with a debugger or the crash, the literal write (usually just a segfault). UBSan with -fsanitize=signed-integer-overflow catches the overflow in lo + hi.

Example: lo=2e9, hi=2.1e9 makes UBSan print "signed integer overflow: 2000000000 + 2100000000 cannot be represented in type int". ASan reports the freed vector buffer with allocation and free stack traces. Writing to a string literal is a write to read-only memory, so it crashes in any build; -Wwrite-strings warns at compile time. Run both sanitizers together in tests.

No. In C++17 the right side of an assignment is sequenced before the left side, so a[i] = i++; is well defined: i++ is evaluated first and the index uses the new value of i.

Example: with i = 0, the right side gives 0 and sets i to 1, then the left side becomes a[1] = 0. Before C++17 it was undefined behaviour (unsequenced read and write of i). It is still unwise to write it, because readers will not know the rule, and f(i, i++) is still only unspecified order.

code.title: Type punning with bit_cast and memcpy

followUps:
Because the compiler may assume pointers of different types do not overlap, it can cache values in registers and reorder loads and stores. If you secretly make them overlap, the cached value goes stale.

int f(int* i, float* f) {
  *i = 1;
  *f = 2.0f;     // compiler assumes i is untouched
  return *i;     // may return 1 without reloading
}

Char types are the exception because they are needed to inspect raw bytes of any object (memcpy, serialisation, allocators), so the standard lets them alias anything. The reverse is not true: reading a char buffer as an int is still UB.

__restrict (a compiler extension in C++) is your promise that, during the pointer's scope, the memory it points to is accessed only through that pointer. This lets the compiler assume no overlap and reorder or vectorise safely.

void add(float* __restrict a, const float* __restrict b, int n) {
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) a[i] += b[i];
}

Without it, the compiler must worry that writing a[i] changes b[i+1], and either emits a runtime overlap check or does not vectorise. If you break the promise (call it with overlapping arrays), behaviour is undefined.

code.title: Toy ASan shadow memory check

followUps:
They share the shadow memory layout and each tool wants to own the shadow mapping and the allocator, and they instrument loads and stores with their own incompatible runtime. So the compiler cannot link both into one binary; run them as separate builds.

Example: ASan marks addresses with a shadow byte (shift by 3). TSan keeps its own shadow cells with thread IDs and clocks for every 8 bytes, at a different address layout. Both also intercept malloc and pthread functions. In CI, run one job with ASan+UBSan and another with TSan.

Container-overflow detection finds accesses to the unused spare capacity inside a container, such as vector elements between size() and capacity(), which are still valid heap memory and so normal ASan would miss them.

Example: vector<int> v; v.reserve(10); v.push_back(1); int x = *(v.data()+5); stays inside the allocation, but ASan with container annotations (libc++ or libstdc++ built with them) poisons bytes past size() and reports container-overflow. It needs the container library to be annotated.

HWASan (hardware-assisted ASan) tags pointers and memory instead of using one shadow byte per 8 bytes: each 16-byte granule gets a small tag, and the top byte of the pointer holds the same tag. A mismatch on access means a bug.

Example: a freed object gets a new tag, so a stale pointer with the old tag fails the check. It uses far less memory (about 10 to 35 percent instead of 2 to 3 times), has no fixed redzone gaps to jump over, and is probabilistic (a 1 in 256 miss chance with 8-bit tags). It needs AArch64 (top-byte ignore) or special x86 support.

Not directly: you cannot instrument code in a pre-built library, so ASan will not see bugs inside it. You can only protect and test the boundary where your code calls it.

Options: build the library from source with the same sanitizer flags (vendor it); use a sanitizer-instrumented libc++ for MSan; run the wrapper code under a fuzzer with ASan on your side so bad inputs trigger bugs at the boundary; use suppression files for known issues; and prefer a hardened allocator or GWP-ASan in production for the uninstrumented parts. MSan in particular gives false positives when it cannot see how the library initialised memory.

Rough overheads: ASan about 2x CPU and 2-3x memory; UBSan 1.2x or less depending on checks; TSan about 5-15x CPU and 5-10x memory; MSan about 3x CPU and 2x memory; LSan almost nothing until exit.

Example: a test suite that takes 10 minutes normally takes about 20 minutes under ASan and about 1.5 hours under TSan, so run TSan only on the concurrency tests and nightly. Use -O1 -fno-omit-frame-pointer to keep it fast and traces readable.

Skid is the delay between the instruction that caused a performance event and the instruction the profiler reports, because the CPU is out-of-order and the sample interrupt lands a few instructions later.

Example: a cache-missing load might be blamed on the instruction two or three after it, so the hot line in the report looks wrong. Fixes: use precise events (PEBS on Intel, IBS on AMD, perf record -e cycles:pp) which record the exact instruction pointer, and read source and assembly together instead of trusting a single line.

Use tools that measure waiting, not CPU: sample off-CPU time and count lock hold and wait times. A CPU profile will look idle when threads are blocked on a mutex.

Steps: 1) check context switches with perf stat -e context-switches or pidstat -w; 2) record off-CPU stacks with eBPF (offcputime) or perf sched; 3) use a lock profiler (perf lock, mutex instrumentation, or Tracy) to see which lock has the longest wait. Then shrink the critical section, shard the lock, or use read-write locks. For example, a map lock held for 5 ms while parsing should be held only for the 50 µs insert.

They show the same data, drawn in opposite directions: a flame graph puts the root at the bottom and grows upward, while an icicle graph hangs from the top and grows downward. Width means time (samples) in both.

Example: the same stack main - handle - parse - alloc appears as four stacked boxes with main at the bottom in a flame graph, and with main at the top in an icicle graph. Icicle layouts are common in tools where the call tree reads like a text outline, and are easier when stacks are shallow and wide. Look for wide boxes at the leaf end in both.

code.title: Microbenchmark with DoNotOptimize and repetitions

followUps:
Latency is the time for one call; throughput is calls per second over many. Measure latency by timing a single call with a dependency chain (the output feeds the next input), and throughput by running many independent calls back-to-back.

Example: a multiply may have latency 3 cycles but throughput of 1 per cycle if calls are independent. Timing x = f(x) in a loop gives latency; timing y[i] = f(a[i]) gives throughput. In Google Benchmark, use a loop with a dependency for latency, and report items_per_second with SetItemsProcessed for throughput. For services, use percentiles (p50, p99) rather than averages.

Because moving code shifts where loops and branch targets sit relative to 16/32/64-byte fetch and cache-line boundaries, which changes how many instruction-fetch blocks, decoder-cache (uop cache) entries and branch-predictor slots they use.

Example: adding an unrelated function earlier in the file moves a hot loop by 20 bytes, so it now straddles a 64-byte boundary and needs two fetches per iteration, giving a few percent slowdown with identical source logic. To compare fairly, repeat across builds, use -falign-loops=32 or similar, or look at many benchmarks rather than one.

code.title: Amdahl's law calculator

followUps:
About 1.67x. Use Amdahl: with p = 0.6 and s = 3 the speed-up is 1 / ((1 - 0.6) + 0.6/3) = 1 / (0.4 + 0.2) = 1 / 0.6 = 1.667.

The new run time is 60 percent of the old one: the untouched 40 units stay, and the 60 units become 20. Even an infinite speed-up would give at most 1 / 0.4 = 2.5x. So a 3x gain on a 60 percent function yields a bit under 2x overall.

Because once one part gets faster, the unchanged parts take a larger share of the total, and the bottleneck can move to something that was hidden before.

Example: a program runs 100 s, of which function A takes 60 s. After making A 3x faster it takes 20 s, so the total is 60 s and A is now only 33 percent, while B (40 s) is 67 percent. Optimising A again helps much less than optimising B. Optimisation can also change behaviour such as cache use or contention, so re-profile after every change.

code.title: Saturating add, checked access and zero-init

followUps:
A hardened library adds cheap checks (bounds, null, precondition) that cost a few percent in most real programs, not the 2x or more of a sanitizer.

Reported numbers: Google measured about 0.3 percent average overhead across its fleet after enabling libc++ hardening, and typical benchmarks show 0.5 to 5 percent, higher in tight loops that index heavily because the check can block vectorisation. A failed check traps immediately (an abort) instead of silently corrupting memory. Measure on your own workload; on hot inner loops you can use unchecked access or iterators after validating the range once.

Because most serious security flaws in C and C++ are memory-safety bugs (out-of-bounds, use-after-free), and memory-safe languages make those bugs impossible or turn them into a safe error by default, rather than relying on discipline.

Example: studies by large vendors found that around 70 percent of their serious vulnerabilities were memory-safety issues. Government agencies therefore recommend memory-safe languages (Rust, Go, C#, Java, Swift) for new code, and a roadmap for existing C++ code. Rewriting is costly, so C++ is adding hardening, profiles and bounds checks as a lower-cost middle path.
